cases.holding: A physician who gave the DHS child-abuse investigator his honest opinion that the father's explanation of an infant's spiral fracture was plausible was immune from civil liability under Iowa Code section 232.73, because that immunity turns on the subjective good faith of the person reporting or assisting in the assessment, not on whether he was negligent.
cases.quote: To avoid summary judgment, the plaintiff must have evidence the defendant acted dishonestly, not merely carelessly, in assisting the DHS.

relevance.INP-01: Sets Iowa's controlling standard for reporter and participant immunity under Iowa Code section 232.73 — subjective good faith, not reasonableness — which is the liability rule every mandatory reporter operates under.
relevance.INP-02: The section 232.73 immunity the court construes extends to any person who makes a report or assists in the assessment, not just to enumerated mandatory reporters.
relevance.INP-06: Because immunity turns on subjective honesty rather than accuracy, a hotline caller acting on an honest belief is protected even if the belief was carelessly formed.
relevance.INP-07: The case arose from a treating physician's communications with the DHS investigator, and the court construed the immunity liberally to encourage exactly those medical-provider disclosures.
relevance.INP-08: Applies the same good-faith immunity framework that governs school and other professional reporters who supply information to a DHS assessment.
relevance.ACT-06: The child was left in the father's care after the physician's assessment input, illustrating how medical judgments at the emergency-care stage drive the agency's protective decision and the immunity that attaches to them.
relevance.DEC-02: The opinion describes how DHS elicits and relies on professional input during a child-abuse assessment, and holds that second-guessing that input is not actionable absent dishonesty.
relevance.FAIL-04: The infant later suffered a severe brain injury after being left with the father, and the court held the physician was nonetheless immune — the leading Iowa authority on civil exposure when a child is harmed after a missed assessment.
relevance.OUT-06: Addresses liability where serious injury follows a child-abuse assessment, holding good-faith participants are not answerable in damages.

cases.case_name: Geringer v. Iowa Department of Human Services
cases.holding: In a contested case brought to expunge a child-abuse report from the central registry, the DHS director was not disqualified from reviewing the ALJ's proposed decision on the agency's own motion, and the mother received all the process she was due.
cases.quote: We also find no denial of due process of law in the manner in which Ellen's claim was adjudicated by the agency.

relevance.INP-01: Confirms that a professional's child-abuse report (here a physician's Munchausen-by-proxy affidavit) is tested through the chapter 17A contested-case route, not collaterally.
relevance.INP-09: Shows the limits of challenging agency self-review: internal recommendations that the director revisit a proposed decision are not disqualifying advocacy.
relevance.INP-10: Illustrates how an accepted report escalates into a registry entry and what internal agency review of that escalation looks like.
relevance.DEC-01: Explains the statutory 'unfounded' and 'undetermined' classifications under Iowa Code section 235A.18(2) and the director's authority to revise an ALJ's unfounded finding.
relevance.DEC-03: The leading Iowa Supreme Court decision on the due-process content of the contested-case hearing that follows a founded or undetermined child-abuse finding.
relevance.FAIL-01: Marks the boundary of judicial reversal of an agency finding: bias or improper combination of functions must be shown, not merely an adverse outcome.
relevance.FAIL-06: Addresses expungement and retention of registry information as the mechanism through which agency records are corrected.
relevance.PMC-02: Demonstrates that Iowa audits its own child-abuse determinations through agency-initiated review under Iowa Code section 17A.15(3).
relevance.PMC-03: Relevant to any citizen-review or independent-panel argument, since the court rejected the claim that agency adjudicators must meet the full judicial conduct canons.
relevance.PMC-05: Confirms registry data is handled through statutory expungement timelines rather than general disclosure.
relevance.PMC-06: Provides the Iowa baseline that agency determinations are reviewable, but only on the record and within chapter 17A's framework.

cases.holding: Iowa Code section 235A.18(2), which requires the central registry to retain a record of an unfounded child-abuse accusation for six months before expungement, does not violate the accused's due-process, privacy, or equal-protection rights.
cases.quote: We think the statute strikes a proper balance between the state's compelling interest in protecting children against abuse and the individual's interest in privacy and reputation.

relevance.INP-01: Upholds the reporting-and-registry system that mandatory reporters feed, on the ground that the state's interest in child protection justifies the intrusion.
relevance.INP-02: Confirms that even an accusation ultimately found unfounded is lawfully recorded, which is the risk any third-party reporter's tip creates for the accused.
relevance.INP-06: Supports the confidentiality architecture behind anonymous hotline reporting: registry information is highly confidential and unauthorized disclosure is criminal.
relevance.INP-07: Applies to medical-origin allegations of sexual abuse recorded in the registry and the accused's inability to compel immediate expungement.
relevance.DEC-01: The controlling Iowa authority on what happens after an unfounded disposition — six-month retention, then expungement — and why that does not offend due process.
relevance.DEC-03: Sets the constitutional floor against which founded findings and their registry consequences are measured, including the holding that reputation alone is not a protected due-process interest.
relevance.OUT-05: Establishes that dismissal or an unfounded outcome does not entitle the accused to immediate erasure of the record.
relevance.FAIL-06: Defines the confidentiality and criminal-penalty regime governing improper disclosure of registry information.
relevance.PMC-03: Frames the state-interest side of the balance any citizen-review body must weigh in evaluating registry policy.
relevance.PMC-04: Supplies the Iowa Supreme Court's statement of the state's compelling interest in child protection, the premise of fatality-review and prevention work.
relevance.PMC-05: Identifies the statutory confidentiality bar (Iowa Code sections 235A.15, 235A.21) that limits public access to child-abuse registry records.

cases.holding: A father ordered out of the family home on a DHS worker's ex parte affidavit, where the abuse allegation was later deemed unfounded, could not recover on tort or state constitutional claims: the affidavit contained no knowing or reckless falsehood, the conduct did not shock the conscience, and the adversary process that cleared him satisfied procedural due process.
cases.quote: One can second-guess Siver's investigation, though, without treating it as a Fourth Amendment violation.

relevance.INP-02: A child's disclosure relayed by a parent in a custody dispute triggered the assessment; the court held the worker could rely on the forensic interview she personally observed.
relevance.INP-03: Describes the forensic-interview-based intake pathway and holds that a caseworker's reliance on it, without further corroboration, is not unconstitutional.
relevance.INP-06: Confirms that an initial report need not be independently corroborated before the agency acts, so long as the affidavit contains no intentional or reckless falsehood.
relevance.INP-10: Governs the escalation from accepted report to ex parte court application, and the standard for attacking that escalation after the fact.
relevance.DEC-01: The allegation was ultimately deemed unfounded, and the court treated that later result as vindication of the process rather than proof of a violation.
relevance.DEC-02: Holds that an incomplete or criticizable investigation is not itself a constitutional tort under article I, section 8 or the Fourth Amendment.
relevance.DEC-03: Holds the father's procedural due process claim fails because the adversary proceeding that set aside the DHS finding was the process he was due.
relevance.ACT-05: The remedy here was an ex parte order removing the alleged abuser from the home rather than removing the children, and the court analyzed that order under the same Fourth Amendment framework.
relevance.OUT-05: Establishes that a later unfounded determination and case dismissal do not, standing alone, generate damages liability against the State or its workers.
relevance.FAIL-02: The leading recent Iowa Supreme Court decision on damages claims arising from an allegedly wrongful DHS-initiated removal or exclusion order, applying a Franks-style falsity requirement.

cases.holding: Social workers have absolute immunity under section 1983 when acting as prosecutors (filing a CINA petition) or as ordinary witnesses, and qualified immunity when acting as complaining witnesses or performing investigatory acts; summary judgment for the State and its workers was affirmed on both the section 1983 and Iowa Tort Claims Act theories.
cases.quote: Similarly, a social worker is entitled to qualified immunity for his or her investigatory acts.

relevance.INP-04: Sets out the immunity consequences that attach once a court-supervised juvenile proceeding is opened at the agency's instance.
relevance.DEC-02: Holds investigatory conduct by a DHS worker is shielded by qualified, not absolute, immunity — the operative liability rule at the investigation stage.
relevance.DEC-04: Establishes the immunity framework applicable to the worker's affidavit supporting a temporary removal order.
relevance.DEC-05: The controlling Iowa authority that filing a CINA petition is a prosecutorial act carrying absolute immunity.
relevance.FAIL-02: The leading Iowa Supreme Court decision on wrongful-removal damages claims against DHS workers under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and the Iowa Tort Claims Act.
relevance.FAIL-04: Also disposes of the claim that the workers negligently failed to protect the child from abuse by a foster parent after placement.
relevance.OUT-06: Addresses agency exposure where a child is harmed in a state-arranged foster placement.
relevance.PMC-04: Illustrates the narrow judicial remedy available after harm in care, which is why administrative fatality and near-fatality review carries the accountability burden.

cases.case_name: F.K. v. Iowa District Court for Polk County
cases.holding: Iowa Code section 232.78, which permits ex parte temporary removal orders on an application that need not be sworn or written, violates neither the Fourth Amendment nor the Warrant Clause nor federal or state due process, because the removal is limited in duration and a reasonably prompt post-removal hearing follows.
cases.quote: On balance, we cannot say that the protections in place in section 232.78 deprive litigants, such as Felicia, of due process.

relevance.INP-04: Describes the ex parte judicial application mechanism by which DHS obtains an order and the limited judicial scrutiny that precedes it.
relevance.INP-12: The controlling Iowa decision on the constitutionality of emergency protective custody under Iowa Code section 232.78, including the ten-day maximum for an ex parte removal.
relevance.DEC-04: Directly governs the constitutional adequacy of the emergency removal decision and the ex parte process supporting it.
relevance.ACT-03: Explains that the post-removal hearing under section 232.95(1) determines only whether removal should continue, not whether the initial removal was proper.
relevance.ACT-05: Confirms the juvenile court's authority to issue immediate ex parte protective orders on a non-sworn application, subject to prompt review.

cases.holding: Adjudicatory, ex parte removal, and dispositional orders were affirmed; by failing to file a timely rule 179(b) motion the mother waived her due-process and statutory objections to deficiencies in the dispositional order, and clear and convincing evidence supported the CINA adjudication.
cases.quote: Similarly, we hold rule 179(b) applies to juvenile court CINA proceedings.

relevance.INP-04: Establishes that objections to how a juvenile court ordered removal or disposition must be raised in that court before they can be pressed on appeal.
relevance.INP-12: Confirms that a post-removal hearing cannot 'go back in time and restore custody based on alleged errors in the initial removal order.'
relevance.DEC-05: Recognizes parents' procedural due-process rights in CINA and termination proceedings while allocating the burden of preserving them.
relevance.ACT-03: Addresses the statutory findings required for a dispositional order placing a child in DHS custody for foster care.
relevance.FAIL-01: The key Iowa error-preservation rule limiting appellate reversal of CINA orders — unpreserved defects, even constitutional ones, are waived.

cases.holding: The reasonable-efforts requirement is not a freestanding substantive element of termination; it bears on the State's burden to prove the child cannot safely be returned home, and a parent who does not object to services early in the case cannot rely on their inadequacy at the termination hearing.
cases.quote: The State must show reasonable efforts as a part of its ultimate proof the child cannot be safely returned to the care of a parent.

relevance.INP-05: Explains that Iowa's reasonable-efforts scheme is built to prevent and eliminate the need for removal, the statutory home for voluntary, front-end help.
relevance.ACT-01: Holds that the focus is on the services actually offered and the parent's response, so a parent who accepts a voluntary plan and does not object cannot later attack its adequacy.
relevance.ACT-02: The leading Iowa statement of the content of the court-ordered reasonable-efforts obligation under Iowa Code section 232.102, including visitation.
relevance.DEC-06: Traces the federal family-preservation-to-ASFA shift that underlies Iowa's non-court service pathways and the waiver of reasonable efforts for aggravated circumstances.
relevance.OUT-01: Defines the reunification obligation — DHS must 'make every reasonable effort to return the child to the child's home as quickly as possible consistent with the best interests of the child.'
relevance.FAIL-03: Explains that the reasonable-efforts requirement exists both to protect parents and children and to preserve the state's federal IV-E matching funds.
relevance.PMC-01: Ties Iowa's reasonable-efforts doctrine directly to the federal funding and performance framework that CFSR measures.
relevance.PMC-02: Identifies the federal financial-incentive rationale for reasonable efforts, the audit hook for IV-E claiming.
relevance.PMC-06: Supplies the doctrinal anchor for any cross-analysis of Iowa's compliance with federal reasonable-efforts mandates.

cases.holding: A father who never asked the juvenile court for different services — complaining only to a social worker — waived his challenge to the adequacy of reunification services, and the State's reasonable efforts were sufficient to support termination.
cases.quote: In general, if a parent fails to request other services at the proper time, the parent waives the issue and may not later challenge it at the termination proceeding.

relevance.ACT-01: Holds that a parent who is dissatisfied with voluntary or offered services must demand alternatives from the court, not merely grumble to the caseworker.
relevance.DEC-06: Sets the timing rule for objecting to a service-based, non-court response: at removal, when the case permanency plan is entered, or at review hearings.
relevance.OUT-01: The controlling Iowa waiver rule that shapes whether a failed reunification can later be blamed on inadequate services.

cases.holding: Termination of an incarcerated mother's parental rights was affirmed: her appellate complaint that DHS never arranged prison visitation came too late because she repeatedly declined to object when the juvenile court asked, and clear and convincing evidence showed the child could not be returned to her.
cases.quote: We conclude Katherine's challenge on appeal to the failure of DHS to provide visitation during her incarceration at the ICIW comes too late.

relevance.ACT-02: Applies the reasonable-efforts waiver rule to court-ordered service plans where visitation is left to DHS discretion and counsel voices no objection.
relevance.OUT-01: Shows how an unexercised right to reunification services — here prison visitation — forecloses a reunification argument at termination.

cases.holding: Where the juvenile court waited twenty months after the evidentiary hearing to enter a written termination order, it abused its discretion by refusing the mother's motion to reopen the record with contemporary evidence of sobriety, housing, and employment; the termination order was reversed and remanded.
cases.quote: We reiterate for emphasis that DHS's reasonable efforts obligation continues until either a final written termination order or a waiver by the juvenile court

relevance.ACT-02: Fixes the endpoint of the court-ordered services obligation: DHS must keep working the plan until the written termination order or a judicial waiver.
relevance.OUT-01: Holds that reunification efforts cannot be abandoned on an oral indication of intent to terminate while the permanency goal on paper remains reunification.
relevance.FAIL-01: A leading Iowa Supreme Court reversal of a juvenile court order for procedural error — inordinate delay plus refusal to reopen the record.
relevance.FAIL-03: Notes the tension between the court's written orders and the services actually delivered, the kind of gap federal reviews are designed to surface.
relevance.PMC-01: Demonstrates judicial enforcement of the continuing reasonable-efforts duty that federal permanency timelines presuppose.

cases.holding: Termination of the mother's rights to both children under Iowa Code section 232.116(1)(h) was proper on clear and convincing evidence; the court restated the governing three-step framework — statutory ground, best-interest factors, then permissive exceptions.
cases.quote: Our review of termination of parental rights under Iowa Code chapter 232 is a three-step analysis.

relevance.OUT-02: States the three-step Iowa termination framework and the definition of clear and convincing evidence that controls every termination decision.
relevance.OUT-06: The CPS case opened after the children's infant sibling died while under the father's supervision, and that death drove the safety analysis.
relevance.FAIL-04: Shows how a child fatality in the household is treated evidentially in subsequent proceedings concerning the surviving siblings.

cases.holding: The court restated and modified the analytical framework for termination to track the text of Iowa Code section 232.116, adopted de novo review for all termination decisions, and affirmed the termination of the father's rights.
cases.quote: The first step in our analysis is to determine if a ground for termination exists under section 232.116(1).

relevance.OUT-02: The foundational modern Iowa case restructuring termination analysis around the statutory text and fixing de novo review for all termination appeals.

cases.holding: Termination under Iowa Code section 232.116(1)(i) was supported by clear and convincing evidence, and the 1998 amendment to section 232.116(2) giving primary consideration to the child's safety and need for a permanent home violates neither procedural nor substantive due process.
cases.quote: Thus, the parents in this case are clearly entitled to procedural due process: notice and a meaningful opportunity to be heard.

relevance.DEC-05: States the minimum process owed to parents once the State opens a juvenile case — notice and a meaningful opportunity to be heard — and upholds the statutory best-interest standard against due-process attack.

cases.holding: Termination of a neglectful mother's rights to her ten-year-old son was affirmed; although Iowa prefers to keep siblings together and values family integrity, those preferences yield to clear and convincing evidence that the child's best interests require a permanent, stable adoptive home.
cases.quote: However, this preference is not absolute. Our ultimate concern is the best interests of the child.

relevance.ACT-03: Confirms that a sibling-separating foster or adoptive placement is permissible when the child's best interests require it.
relevance.ACT-04: The controlling Iowa statement of the sibling-placement preference and its limits when weighed against permanency.
relevance.OUT-03: Explains why continued placement with family cannot override a clear showing that permanency elsewhere serves the child.

cases.holding: A father's physical abuse of other family members and history of domestic violence, without direct abuse of the child, supported adjudicating the child a child in need of assistance under Iowa Code section 232.2(6)(b) and (c)(2).
cases.quote: Under Iowa Code section 232.96(2), the State bears the burden of proving its allegations by clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.DEC-02: Defines the evidentiary threshold the agency must be building toward from the assessment stage forward in a CINA case.
relevance.DEC-03: States the clear-and-convincing burden at adjudication, which is materially higher than the preponderance standard governing an administrative founded finding.
relevance.ACT-05: Holds that domestic violence directed at other household members, without direct injury to the child, can itself justify protective juvenile court intervention.

cases.holding: The Iowa ICWA placement preferences in chapter 232B are unconstitutional as applied in voluntary termination cases, so the federal ICWA preferences and their 'good cause' exception for a parent's request govern; a tribe may also appear through a non-lawyer authorized representative.
cases.quote: The Iowa ICWA placement preferences are unconstitutional in voluntary termination cases.

relevance.INP-11: The controlling Iowa Supreme Court decision on when state ICWA yields to federal ICWA and on tribal participation rights in Iowa child-custody proceedings.
relevance.ACT-04: Determines which placement-preference hierarchy applies to an Indian child — federal, not Iowa — in voluntary proceedings, and preserves the 'good cause' deviation.
relevance.FAIL-05: Limits the reach of Iowa's tribe-favoring placement scheme where it would override a consenting parent's choice, the Iowa authority on the constitutional ceiling of ICWA-based preferences.

cases.holding: Termination of parental rights to an Indian child was affirmed: the tribe was notified immediately, active efforts to prevent the breakup of the Indian family were made, and the Iowa ICWA requirements including qualified expert testimony and proof beyond a reasonable doubt were satisfied.
cases.quote: Even assuming the issue was properly preserved, we conclude active efforts were made to prevent the breakup of the Indian family.

relevance.INP-11: Published Iowa appellate authority applying the chapter 232B active-efforts, tribal-notice, and qualified-expert-witness requirements once an Indian child is identified.
relevance.ACT-02: Illustrates what satisfies the heightened 'active efforts' service obligation owed to the parents of an Indian child, as distinct from reasonable efforts.
relevance.ACT-04: Addresses the father's challenge that placement was not decided until after the termination hearing, under the Iowa ICWA placement framework.

cases.holding: Limiting an incarcerated mother's telephone participation in her termination hearing to her own testimony was error; going forward juvenile courts must let incarcerated parents participate by phone in the entire hearing, and the termination order was reversed and remanded.
cases.quote: Juvenile judges must give incarcerated parents the opportunity to participate by telephone in the entire hearing.

relevance.OUT-02: The controlling Iowa rule on an incarcerated parent's right to participate in the whole termination hearing, not just to testify.
relevance.FAIL-05: Corrects a participation practice that systematically disadvantaged incarcerated parents, the closest Iowa analogue to a status-based procedural inequity holding.

cases.holding: In a private chapter 600A termination brought by the mother against the incarcerated father, the mother failed to prove by clear and convincing evidence that terminating the father's rights would advance the children's best interests, and the termination decree was reversed.
cases.quote: we conclude A.P. did not show by clear and convincing evidence the best interest of the children will be advanced by termination of B.G.'s parental rights

relevance.OUT-03: Holds that a stable alternative caregiving arrangement does not by itself justify severing the other parent's legal relationship, a key limit on permanency-by-substitution.
relevance.OUT-05: The leading recent Iowa decision refusing termination and leaving the parent-child relationship intact where the petitioner's proof fell short.

cases.holding: The element that a child has been 'removed from the physical custody' of a parent for twelve of the last eighteen months under Iowa Code section 232.116(1)(e) and (f) requires an actual change from physical custody to lack of physical custody; mere absence of custody does not satisfy it, and the termination was reversed.
cases.quote: Certainly such absence of physical custody would not provide the necessary predicate for a termination of parental rights under section 232.116(1)(e) and (f).

relevance.ACT-01: The father's family participated in voluntary services after a founded assessment and the case closed, showing how a voluntary-service episode fits (or fails to fit) the statutory removal clock.
relevance.DEC-06: Demonstrates that a safety plan excluding a parent from the home is not automatically a statutory 'removal' with termination consequences.
relevance.OUT-02: Controls the removal-duration element of the most commonly used Iowa termination grounds and requires prior judicial notice of parenting shortcomings before that clock runs.

cases.holding: Under the 2020 Guardianship Act, when a parent revokes consent and the basis for a minor's guardianship no longer exists, Iowa Code section 232D.503(2) places the burden on the guardian to justify continuing it, and the constitutionally grounded parental preference survived the repeal of the old statutory preference; termination of the guardianship was affirmed.
cases.quote: The constitutionally based parental preference predated section 633.559 and, in our view, survives its repeal.

relevance.INP-05: Governs the consensual guardianship route parents use to arrange temporary care without agency involvement, and their right to unwind it.
relevance.ACT-04: Establishes that a kinship guardian cannot retain a child against a fit parent's wishes merely because the placement has become comfortable.
relevance.OUT-03: The controlling Iowa authority on burden of proof and the parental preference in minor guardianship terminations under chapter 232D.
relevance.OUT-04: Defines how a chapter 232D guardianship — the vehicle for extended kinship permanency — ends and who bears the burden when it is challenged.

cases.holding: An 'established' legal father who is neither the biological nor the adoptive father is not a 'parent' under chapter 232 and therefore is not a necessary party to CINA or termination proceedings; his remedy is to petition to intervene to seek guardianship or custody.
cases.quote: Daniel is neither J.C.'s biological father nor her adoptive father. Although Daniel is J.C.'s established father, he is not her parent under chapter 232.

relevance.INP-05: Identifies who may come forward to seek custody or guardianship of a child already in the system, and by what mechanism.
relevance.DEC-05: The controlling Iowa authority on who must be joined as a necessary party when the State files a CINA or termination petition.
relevance.OUT-03: Preserves a non-parent established father's route to guardianship or custody through post-termination intervention.

cases.holding: A CINA permanency order that changes custody and directs the county attorney to file a termination petition is interlocutory, not a final appealable order, and interlocutory review was denied; the appeal was dismissed.
cases.quote: In sum, we conclude that the order here was interlocutory and that we should deny permission to appeal from it.

relevance.OUT-04: Controls appealability of the permanency orders that set a youth's long-term placement course, including continued out-of-home care.
relevance.FAIL-01: The leading Iowa rule on when a parent may obtain appellate review of a permanency or custody-change order — generally not until final disposition.

cases.case_name: Iowa Department of Health and Human Services v. Iowa District Court for Polk County
cases.holding: A juvenile court acts within its authority under Iowa Code section 232.102(1)(b)(1) when, at an interested party's request, it temporarily stays HHS from moving a child in its custody until it can hold an evidentiary hearing; review of an HHS placement decision may be prospective as well as retrospective.
cases.quote: The juvenile court "shall give deference" to HHS's placement decision, but deference does not mean blind acceptance that freezes the juvenile court out of any meaningful review of HHS's decision.

relevance.INP-09: Defines the scope of independent judicial oversight over agency placement practice, the courtroom counterpart to administrative review.
relevance.ACT-03: The most recent Iowa Supreme Court statement of how far a juvenile court may go in reviewing an HHS foster-placement change.
relevance.ACT-04: Arose from HHS's attempt to move a child to a sibling placement, and addresses the statutory sibling-placement preference against the child's individual best interests.
relevance.OUT-04: Bears on stability of long-term placements, the practical foundation of a youth's path to permanency or extended care.
relevance.FAIL-01: Reverses an appellate ruling that had stripped the juvenile court of prospective review, restoring judicial power to check agency placement decisions.
relevance.FAIL-03: Notes HHS's failure to articulate a concurrent permanency plan and its earlier attempt to place children in a home without running water or electricity.
relevance.PMC-01: Provides a recent, concrete judicial record of Iowa placement-practice deficiencies relevant to federal safety and permanency monitoring.

cases.holding: The CINA adjudication and foster placement of an infant were affirmed; the mother's Americans with Disabilities Act reasonable-accommodation claim was not preserved because it was never raised in the juvenile court, and in any event the providers offered were trained to work with her personality disorder.
cases.quote: As a general rule, an issue not presented in the juvenile court may not be raised for the first time on appeal.

relevance.INP-07: The case began with an emergency removal at the hospital based on nursing staff's concerns about the mother's capacity to care for her newborn.
relevance.ACT-06: Involved medication non-compliance amounting to denial of critical care and the resulting protective response to the infant's medical needs.
relevance.FAIL-05: The principal published Iowa appellate decision addressing an ADA reasonable-accommodation claim by a disabled parent in a child-welfare case, and the preservation rule that defeats such claims raised late.

cases.case_name: ACLU Foundation of Iowa, Inc. v. Records Custodian, Atlantic Community School District
cases.holding: Information about the discipline imposed on two school employees who strip-searched five students is personal information in confidential personnel records exempt from disclosure under Iowa Code section 22.7(11); no balancing test applies once information fits a statutory exemption.
cases.quote: we hold that the disciplinary information sought is exempt from disclosure under Iowa Code section 22.7(11)

relevance.INP-08: Concerns school-employee misconduct against students and shows that the resulting disciplinary record is shielded from the public even where the incident is a matter of public concern.
relevance.INP-09: Establishes that Iowa's open-records law will not itself supply the transparency needed to audit how institutions handled suspected child mistreatment.
relevance.FAIL-06: The controlling Iowa authority on statutory exemptions to chapter 22 disclosure and the courts' refusal to balance the public interest against them.
relevance.PMC-02: Confirms that personnel-file exemptions block public access to individual accountability records in Iowa agencies and districts.
relevance.PMC-03: Marks the statutory limits any citizen review effort will encounter when seeking Iowa records about individual staff conduct.
relevance.PMC-04: Shows that fatality- or incident-review transparency in Iowa must come from a specific disclosure statute, not from chapter 22.
relevance.PMC-05: The leading Iowa Open Records Act case: if information fits an exemption, the court directs policy arguments for disclosure to the legislature.
relevance.PMC-06: Defines the legal ceiling on what Iowa child-welfare records an outside analyst can lawfully obtain.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Before a State may sever completely and irrevocably the rights of parents in their natural child, the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment requires the State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence; New York's fair-preponderance standard was unconstitutional.
cases.quote: We hold that such a standard adequately conveys to the factfinder the level of subjective certainty about his factual conclusions necessary to satisfy due process.

relevance.OUT-02: The federal constitutional floor for the burden of proof at termination, which Iowa Code section 232.117(3) and every Iowa termination decision implement.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: A state child-protection agency's failure to remove a child from a father it knew or suspected was abusing him did not deprive the child of liberty in violation of the Due Process Clause, because the Clause imposes no affirmative constitutional duty on the State to protect against private violence.
cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

relevance.OUT-06: The controlling federal rule that a child gravely injured by a parent after CPS involvement generally has no substantive due-process damages claim against the agency.
relevance.FAIL-04: Sets the constitutional baseline against which every claim arising from a child's death or serious injury under agency supervision must be measured.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Due process does not require appointment of counsel for an indigent parent in every parental-rights termination proceeding; the decision is left in the first instance to the trial court, subject to appellate review, and no error occurred on these facts.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.DEC-05: Sets the federal constitutional floor for appointed counsel once the State petitions to end the parent-child relationship — a floor Iowa exceeds by statute.
relevance.OUT-02: Establishes that the federal right to appointed counsel at termination is case-by-case, making Iowa's statutory guarantee the operative protection.

cases.case_name: Mitchell v. Dakota County Social Services
cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: A father's substantive due-process claims against county child-protection staff failed: reliance on circumstantial allegations of abuse, an assertedly improper investigation, and a caseworker's unprofessional remarks do not amount to conscience-shocking conduct.
cases.quote: such reliance is not an egregious abuse of power that shocks the conscience

relevance.INP-10: Holds that escalating an investigation on circumstantial allegations, without independent corroboration, is not a constitutional violation in this circuit.
relevance.DEC-02: The governing Eighth Circuit standard for attacking the quality of a child-abuse investigation on substantive due-process grounds.
relevance.FAIL-02: Defines how high the bar sits in the Eighth Circuit — which includes Iowa — for damages claims premised on investigative misconduct short of a seizure.

cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: Des Moines detectives conducting a child welfare check were not entitled to qualified immunity for arresting a mother on her porch after she refused their demands: without a warrant, an exigency, a removal order, or her consent, they could neither enter the home nor compel her to produce the child.
cases.quote: they could not lawfully enter the home without Webster's consent, nor force her to take any specific action with respect to L.B.

relevance.INP-03: An Iowa case decided by Iowa's federal circuit, defining the lawful limits of a law-enforcement child welfare check that precedes a CPS referral.
relevance.INP-12: Confirms that taking protective custody requires a warrant, court order, consent, or a genuine exigency — the four lawful doors.
relevance.DEC-04: Reiterates the Eighth Circuit rule that the exigent circumstances permitting removal without a court order are 'extremely limited.'
relevance.FAIL-02: The most recent Eighth Circuit qualified-immunity decision arising in Iowa on unlawful entry and coercion during a child welfare check.

cases.case_name: Heartland Academy Community Church v. Waddle
cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: The Eighth Circuit affirmed injunctive relief and the district court's conclusion that a juvenile officer's mass removal of children from a residential school violated the Fourth Amendment — the ex parte orders were tainted by the manner in which they were obtained, and thirty-five children were taken with no court order, probable cause, or exigent circumstances.
cases.quote: upon de novo review, we see no error in the legal conclusions on the reasonableness of the seizures and the Fourth Amendment violation

relevance.INP-12: The Eighth Circuit's clearest condemnation of mass protective custody taken without individualized court authorization or exigency.
relevance.DEC-04: Establishes that both the absence of a court order and the improper procurement of an ex parte order can render an emergency removal unreasonable.
relevance.FAIL-02: Leading circuit authority that removals lacking probable cause or exigency are unconstitutional seizures, and that prospective injunctive relief is available.

cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: A county social worker who obtained an ex parte order removing a high school student for a seventy-two-hour psychiatric evaluation after his teacher reported a violent murder-suicide essay was entitled to qualified immunity, and the mother's familial-association claim failed because there was no underlying Fourth Amendment violation.
cases.quote: Diercks had a "reasonable suspicion" of a threat to David's welfare that justified the ex parte order removing David from his home

relevance.INP-03: Illustrates the coordinated school-to-law-enforcement-to-child-protection referral chain and the reasonable-suspicion standard that validates the resulting order.
relevance.INP-08: Directly on point for educator-originated reports: a teacher's report of a student's writing was a lawful basis for protective intervention.
relevance.ACT-06: Upholds a court-ordered emergency psychiatric evaluation and seventy-two-hour hold as consistent with the Fourth Amendment on a reasonable suspicion of danger.

cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: The Eighth Circuit affirmed the denial of qualified immunity on a motion to dismiss where a child-abuse investigator was alleged to have ordered seven children removed from their home despite contrary evidence and staff recommendations; reasonable suspicion of child abuse is required and is judged on the totality of the circumstances at the time of removal.
cases.quote: whether there was reasonable suspicion of child abuse warranting removal must be determined by analyzing the totality of the circumstances at the time of the removal

relevance.INP-12: States the substantive standard — reasonable suspicion of child abuse on the totality of the circumstances — that must exist when protective custody is taken.
relevance.DEC-04: The governing Eighth Circuit test for whether an emergency removal decision had an adequate factual basis.
relevance.FAIL-02: Confirms that a removal ordered against the weight of the investigator's own evidence can defeat qualified immunity in Iowa's circuit.

cases.holding: Reinstating the juvenile court's order terminating both parents' rights to a one-year-old under Iowa Code section 232.116(1)(h), the court found clear and convincing evidence the child could not be safely returned, held termination was in her best interests, and concluded that none of the permissive grounds in section 232.116(3) — including the relative-legal-custody exception in (3)(a) and the closeness-of-relationship exception in (3)(c) — applied.
cases.quote: A finding under subsection 3 allows the court not to terminate.

relevance.OUT-02: Supplies what the brief otherwise lacked at step three of the Iowa termination analysis: the Iowa Supreme Court's own application of the section 232.116(3) permissive exceptions, which is where most Iowa termination appeals are actually decided.
relevance.OUT-03: Holds that a child's placement with, and bond to, grandparents who are not her legal custodians does not trigger the section 232.116(3)(a) relative-custody exception, marking the limit of kinship-based arguments against termination.

cases.holding: On de novo review the court affirmed termination of the mother's rights under Iowa Code section 232.116(1)(d) and (h), articulating the three-step chapter 232 analysis — statutory ground, then the section 232.116(2) best-interest framework, then the section 232.116(3) permissive exceptions — and finding no exception applied.
cases.quote: We will uphold an order terminating parental rights if there is clear and convincing evidence of grounds for termination under Iowa Code section 232.116.

relevance.OUT-02: This is the source decision for the three-step framework and the clear-and-convincing standard that In re M.W. quotes, so a practitioner citing the framework should cite D.W. rather than a later case repeating it.

cases.holding: A parent's unresolved methamphetamine addiction can by itself support a CINA adjudication under Iowa Code section 232.2(6)(c)(2) because of the 'harmful effects' it produces, but it does not by itself prove the child is 'imminently likely' to suffer nonaccidental physical injury under section 232.2(6)(b); the (b) adjudication was reversed and the balance of the juvenile court's order affirmed.
cases.quote: we do not believe general statements about methamphetamine addiction are enough by themselves to prove that a child is imminently likely to suffer physical harm under section 232.2(6)(b)

relevance.DEC-02: The leading Iowa Supreme Court decision on what an accepted substance-use assessment must actually establish, holding that the statutory CINA grounds are narrowly defined phrases the State must match to specific evidence rather than general propositions about addiction.
relevance.DEC-03: States that CINA determinations must rest on clear and convincing evidence under Iowa Code section 232.96(2) and shows the court enforcing that burden by reversing one adjudication ground while sustaining another.

cases.case_name: McCracken v. Iowa Department of Human Services
cases.holding: DHS had statutory authority to investigate the same alleged incident a second time and to enter a founded report even though an earlier investigation had produced an unfounded report that was expunged; the second investigator lawfully accessed the expunged unfounded information under Iowa Code section 235A.15(3), and the father's constitutional due-process objections to the ALJ hearing were not preserved.
cases.quote: the department had statutory authority to conduct an investigation involving the alleged sexual abuse, even though a previous investigation of the same allegation resulted in an unfounded report

relevance.INP-01: Holds that a department social worker who learns of suspected abuse is herself a mandatory reporter bound by Iowa Code section 232.69 and exposed to civil and criminal penalties for silence, so a new disclosure restarts the reporting duty.
relevance.DEC-01: The direct Iowa authority that an unfounded screening decision and expungement do not create finality — DHS may and must investigate again when new information arrives.
relevance.DEC-02: Establishes that once DHS receives a child-abuse allegation it has no discretion to decline an assessment, which is the statutory engine behind the accept-for-investigation decision.
relevance.OUT-05: Confirms that closing a case as unfounded is not an adjudication on the merits that bars later agency action on the same incident.
relevance.FAIL-06: Construes the Iowa Code section 235A.15 confidentiality scheme and its narrow access exception for the departmental investigator, defining who may lawfully see expunged unfounded information.
relevance.PMC-05: Shows that access to expunged child-abuse information in Iowa is controlled entirely by the enumerated statutory exceptions, not by any general transparency principle.

cases.case_name: Grant v. Iowa Department of Human Services
cases.holding: Issue preclusion may not be used to dismiss an application under Iowa Code section 235A.19 to correct a founded child-abuse assessment merely because a district court in a parallel visitation proceeding already resolved the same predicate fact; the district court judgment was reversed and the case remanded to DHS for a hearing on the correction request.
cases.quote: the legislative policies and goals are best served by allowing the DHS to correct its own assessment of a child abuse report free from the doctrine of issue preclusion

relevance.DEC-01: Explains the Iowa Code section 235A.19 correction procedure by which a subject of a report challenges the department's classification and registry entry.
relevance.DEC-03: The controlling recent Iowa authority on a parent's route to attack a founded finding, holding the department must decide all issues a timely correction request presents rather than deferring to another tribunal's fact-finding.
relevance.FAIL-01: A reversal of an agency dismissal for an erroneous interpretation of law under Iowa Code section 17A.19(10)(c), and a concrete example of the judicial check on a DHS refusal to revisit its own child-abuse determination.
relevance.FAIL-06: Grounds the accuracy-of-records rationale — the public interest in maintaining correct registry data — that drives correction and expungement of erroneous child-abuse information.

cases.holding: Iowa's expedited termination-appeal rules, which require a petition on appeal rather than full briefing, satisfy both equal protection and procedural due process because the parent may identify every issue and the reviewing court has the entire record and transcript for de novo review; counsel was therefore not ineffective for failing to challenge them.
cases.quote: the expedited appellate procedure in termination-of-parental-rights cases that permits only a petition on review rather than full briefing does not violate constitutional requirements of procedural due process or equal protection

relevance.DEC-05: States the Iowa Supreme Court's own procedural-due-process framework for a parent facing State action against the parent-child relationship — a protected liberty interest, notice, and an opportunity to be heard adequate to safeguard it, weighed under Mathews v. Eldridge.
relevance.OUT-02: Confirms that the parent's liberty interest in the care, custody, and control of the child is implicated at termination while holding that Iowa's streamlined appellate review of termination orders is constitutionally adequate.

cases.holding: Although Ohio was the children's home state and an Ohio dissolution court had already entered a temporary custody order, the Iowa juvenile court had subject matter jurisdiction under Iowa Code section 598A.3(1)(b) to adjudicate the children in need of assistance and limit the father to supervised visitation, and clear and convincing evidence of domestic abuse committed in the children's presence supported the adjudication.
cases.quote: the Iowa juvenile court did have subject matter jurisdiction for the limited purpose of protecting the children from risks of harm arising during their presence in this state

relevance.INP-04: The Iowa authority closest to the court-ordered-referral node: a CPS investigation generated inside a contested interstate custody fight, and the court's holding that the UCCJA gets a less restrictive application in juvenile proceedings brought by state welfare agencies so protective jurisdiction is not defeated by a pending dissolution elsewhere.
relevance.ACT-05: Upholds a protective disposition — supervised visitation for the father while physical care remained with the mother — as the intervention short of removing the children from parental care.

notes: Method: 35 cases, all retrieved from CourtListener in this session and read in full text. Search order was Supreme Court of Iowa (court_id iowa) first, then Court of Appeals of Iowa (iowactapp), then the U.S. Supreme Court and the Eighth Circuit (Iowa's federal circuit) where the node turns on a federal standard. 31 of 35 are published opinions of the Iowa Supreme Court, the Iowa Court of Appeals, SCOTUS, or the Eighth Circuit; no unpublished memorandum decisions were used.

The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in every IA node file are keyword-matched noise (e.g. 'In re Davenport Hotel Building Collapse', 'In re the Marriage Kraus', 'In re Estate of Johnston', and long runs of unrelated guardianship listings). None of them survived retrieval and review; every one was discarded. The only overlap with a real, on-point case is generic 'Doe v. Iowa District Court for Polk County' styling, which is unrelated to F.K. v. Iowa District Court for Polk County, the genuine emergency-removal case included here.

Three Iowa Supreme Court opinions in this brief have no reporter citation in the CourtListener cluster and are given in slip form: Lennette v. State, No. 20-1148 (Iowa June 10, 2022); In re Guardianship of L.Y., No. 20-1034 (Iowa Jan. 14, 2022); Iowa Dep't of Health & Human Servs. v. Iowa District Court for Polk County, No. 24-0834 (Iowa Oct. 31, 2025). A practitioner should add the N.W.2d cite before filing.

date_decided values are the cluster's date_filed as recorded by CourtListener. For Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County the cluster records 1981-08-28; the opinion was announced June 1, 1981 and the reported cite is 452 U.S. 18 (1981). Year is unaffected.

OUT-04 (extended foster care / jurisdiction past 18) has NO on-point Iowa appellate authority. Targeted searches for extended foster care, aftercare services, voluntary placement after the eighteenth birthday, and juvenile court jurisdiction past age eighteen returned zero responsive published opinions in either iowa or iowactapp. The three cases mapped to OUT-04 are the closest structural authority — permanency-order appealability (In re T.R.), placement-stability review (Iowa HHS v. Iowa District Court), and chapter 232D guardianship termination (In re Guardianship of L.Y.). Iowa's extended foster care program rests on Iowa Code sections 234.46 and 232.2(6) as amended and appears not yet to have generated published case law.

FAIL-03 (federal compliance failure / CFSR and IV-E penalties) and the PMC family (CFSR monitoring, OIG audit, citizen review panels, fatality review commission, FOIA) have no Iowa case law addressing those federal oversight mechanisms directly. No state has generated much. The cases mapped there are the nearest Iowa authority on the same underlying legal machinery: In re C.B. for the IV-E reasonable-efforts funding condition; the 2025 Iowa HHS placement-review decision for judicial oversight of agency practice; Geringer and Roth for administrative review and registry data handling; and ACLU Foundation of Iowa v. Atlantic Community School District for the Iowa Open Records Act ceiling. Lawyers should treat the federal statutes and 45 C.F.R. part 1355 as the operative authority at those nodes, not these cases.

Iowa has not decided a case squarely holding that a caseworker's warrantless entry into a home to investigate child abuse violates the Fourth Amendment or Iowa Const. art. I, section 8. Lennette expressly assumed without deciding that the federal removal principles apply under article I, section 8, and noted the plaintiff had not argued for a different state standard. The Fourth Amendment content at INP-12, DEC-04 and FAIL-02 therefore comes from the Eighth Circuit (Webster, Stanley v. Finnegan, Heartland Academy, Mitchell) and from F.K.'s holding that the section 232.78 ex parte scheme is facially valid.

On the founded-finding due-process node (DEC-03), note the two-tier standard: Iowa Code section 235A.18 uses preponderance of the evidence for the administrative founded/unfounded determination and the contested-case route under chapter 17A (Geringer, Roth), while a CINA adjudication requires clear and convincing evidence under Iowa Code section 232.96(2) (In re L.H.) and termination requires clear and convincing evidence under section 232.117(3) and Santosky.

The reasonable-efforts waiver rule is the single most outcome-determinative doctrine in Iowa child-welfare litigation: under In re C.B. and In re C.H., a parent who does not demand different services from the juvenile court — not merely from a caseworker — at removal, at the case-permanency-plan stage, or at a review hearing forfeits the argument entirely at termination. In re L.M. applies it to an incarcerated parent denied all visitation. In re L.T. is the counterweight, holding the DHS obligation runs until the final written termination order or a judicial waiver.

Iowa ICWA note for practitioners: In re N.N.E. holds the chapter 232B placement preferences unconstitutional in VOLUNTARY termination cases only, leaving the federal ICWA preferences and their 'good cause' exception to govern there. In involuntary proceedings chapter 232B continues to apply, including the beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard and the qualified-expert-witness requirement of Iowa Code section 232B.6(6)(a), as applied in the published Court of Appeals decision In re D.S. Haaland v. Brackeen, 599 U.S. 255 (2023) was located but not included, because its equal-protection and nondelegation holdings were resolved on standing and it adds nothing Iowa courts have yet applied.

Troxel v. Granville was searched but the CourtListener cluster for 530 U.S. 57 exposed only dissenting opinions as separately retrievable text; rather than quote from a dissent, the parental-liberty-interest proposition is carried here by In re Guardianship of L.Y., which states it as Iowa law and independently grounds it in the Iowa Constitution.

No published Iowa appellate decision was found on missing or absent children from foster care, on child-fatality review commission access, or on retaliation against a reporter or foster parent. Searches for those subjects in both iowa and iowactapp returned nothing responsive. FAIL-05 is served by the only Iowa published decision addressing a disability-discrimination (ADA) defense in a child-welfare case, In re C.M., together with the two ICWA/status cases.

In re C.M. (Iowa Ct. App. 1994) and In re D.S. (Iowa Ct. App. 2011) are the only two intermediate appellate cases used; both are published, and both were selected because no Iowa Supreme Court decision reaches the point (ADA reasonable accommodation for a disabled parent; application of the chapter 232B active-efforts and qualified-expert-witness requirements).

Added In re A.M., 843 N.W.2d 100 (Iowa 2014) (cluster 2687684, opinion retrieved and read in full this session) for OUT-02 and OUT-03: it closes the brief's most serious gap by supplying the Iowa Supreme Court's own step-three analysis under Iowa Code section 232.116(3), holding the subsection-3 factors permissive and rejecting both the relative-legal-custody exception in (3)(a) — inapplicable because the grandparents had physical care but not legal custody — and the closeness-of-relationship exception in (3)(c).

Added In re D.W., 791 N.W.2d 703 (Iowa 2010) (cluster 4472480, opinion 4249733 retrieved and read in full this session) for OUT-02: it is the source decision for the three-step chapter 232 framework and the clear-and-convincing standard that In re M.W. quotes second-hand, so a practitioner citing the framework should cite D.W. directly.

Added In re J.S., 846 N.W.2d 36 (Iowa 2014) (cluster 2687615, majority by Mansfield retrieved and read in full this session; the Cady and Zager dissents were read and excluded from quotation) for DEC-02 and DEC-03: it is the leading Iowa Supreme Court decision on what an accepted substance-use assessment must prove, distinguishing the 'harmful effects' ground in Iowa Code section 232.2(6)(c)(2), which methamphetamine addiction alone can satisfy, from the 'imminently likely to abuse or neglect' ground in section 232.2(6)(b), which it cannot.

Added McCracken v. Iowa Department of Human Services, 595 N.W.2d 779 (Iowa 1999) (cluster 1990166, opinion retrieved and read in full this session) for INP-01, DEC-01, DEC-02, OUT-05, FAIL-06 and PMC-05: it is materially closer to the screen-out and registry nodes than Roth or Geringer because it holds that an unfounded disposition and expungement create no finality, that DHS has no discretion to decline an assessment once an allegation arrives, and that only the enumerated Iowa Code section 235A.15(3) persons may access expunged unfounded information.

Added Grant v. Iowa Department of Human Services, 722 N.W.2d 169 (Iowa 2006) (cluster 1572357, opinion retrieved and read in full this session) for DEC-01, DEC-03, FAIL-01 and FAIL-06: it is the controlling recent authority on a parent's route to correct a founded finding under Iowa Code section 235A.19, holding issue preclusion cannot bar the correction hearing even where a district court in a parallel proceeding resolved the same fact, and reversing the agency dismissal under Iowa Code section 17A.19(10)(c).

Added In re C.M., 652 N.W.2d 204 (Iowa 2002) (cluster 8279378, opinion 8244730 retrieved and read in full this session) for DEC-05 and OUT-02. CAVEAT for readers: the verifier described this case as the Iowa Supreme Court's leading statement of parents' fundamental liberty interest. That is not what it decides. It is a constitutional challenge to Iowa's expedited termination-appeal rules, upheld against equal-protection and procedural-due-process attack. It does state, as a necessary step, that a termination proceeding implicates the parent's protected liberty interest in the care, custody and control of the child and sets out the Mathews v. Eldridge balancing that governs, which is why it earns a place at DEC-05 — but it should not be cited for a broad parental-rights proposition.

Added In re E.A., 552 N.W.2d 135 (Iowa 1996) (cluster 1840805, opinion retrieved and read in full this session) for INP-04 and ACT-05. INP-04 (court-ordered referral) had no Iowa authority at all; E.A. is the closest published Iowa Supreme Court decision, holding that the UCCJA is given a less restrictive application in juvenile proceedings initiated by state welfare agencies so that a pending out-of-state dissolution and a foreign temporary custody order do not defeat Iowa's protective jurisdiction. It remains an imperfect fit: INP-04 as defined (a judge ordering CPS to investigate) has produced no published Iowa opinion, and practitioners should rely on Iowa Code sections 232.71 and 232.71B rather than case law.

All six authorities the verifier named as missing were located, retrieved and read this session; none had to be dropped as unverifiable or off point, though the characterization of In re C.M. (2002) was materially wrong and is corrected in the note above. No authority in this pass failed verification.

node_map correction: the node_map in the reconciled brief was materially under-populated relative to the per-case relevance objects already in it — INP-04, INP-09, OUT-04 and PMC-02 through PMC-06 were listed as empty even though Geringer, Roth, Minor, F.K., A.M.H., In re T.R., Iowa HHS, In re C.B., In re J.C. and the ACLU case each carried explicit relevance sentences for those nodes. The node_map returned here is rebuilt from the relevance objects and then curated so that no node exceeds six cases. Where a node would have overflowed, the least central entry was dropped from node_map only (never from the case's relevance): Nelson v. Lindaman at DEC-02, and Lassiter, In re M.W. and In re C.M. (2002) at OUT-02. Every one of the 42 nodes now carries between two and six cases.

Re-ran the OUT-04 search this session against court_id iowa and iowactapp using 'extended foster care', 'aftercare services', 'age of eighteen' and juvenile-court-jurisdiction phrasings. Zero responsive published child-welfare opinions; the only hits were juvenile-sentencing criminal cases (Seats, Null, Sweet, Lyle line). The earlier finding stands: Iowa has generated no published appellate authority on extended foster care or aging out, and OUT-04 rests on the three structural placement/permanency cases.

Missing (for a later pass): In re A.B., 815 N.W.2d 764 (Iowa 2012) — existence and citation confirmed on CourtListener this pass (Supreme Court of Iowa, filed 2012-06-22). The leading modern Iowa Supreme Court decision on unresolved parental substance abuse as a ground for termination and on looking to the parent's past performance as predictive of future care. Its absence is conspicuous at OUT-02 and DEC-03, and it is the natural companion to In re J.S., 846 N.W.2d 36, on the gap between what addiction proves at adjudication and what it proves at termination.

Missing (for a later pass): Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) — the controlling federal statement of a fit parent's fundamental liberty interest in the care, custody and control of their children. The brief excludes it because the CourtListener cluster exposed only dissents as separately retrievable text. That is a retrieval problem, not a reason to omit a controlling Supreme Court authority; the plurality is readily citable and the proposition is uncontested. It belongs at DEC-05, OUT-02 and OUT-03, and In re Guardianship of L.Y. is a poor substitute for it.

Missing (for a later pass): Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976) — the three-factor procedural-due-process balancing test. In re C.M., 652 N.W.2d 204 (Iowa 2002), verified this pass, applies it expressly, and Geringer, Lennette and In re K.M. all turn on it. The brief invokes Mathews by name in its notes but never lists it as an authority, leaving DEC-03 and DEC-05 without the test their Iowa cases actually run.

Missing (for a later pass): Haaland v. Brackeen, 599 U.S. 255 (2023) — the brief located it and excluded it on the stated ground that its holdings 'were resolved on standing.' That is only partly accurate: the Court rejected the Article I and anticommandeering challenges to ICWA on the merits and upheld the statute, dismissing only the equal-protection and nondelegation claims for want of standing. Any practitioner briefing INP-11 or ACT-04 in 2026 must address it, and INP-11 currently rests on only two cases with no margin.

Missing (for a later pass): Manzano v. South Dakota Department of Social Services, 60 F.3d 505 (8th Cir. 1995) — the foundational Eighth Circuit decision on caseworker qualified immunity and the reasonableness of removing a child from the home, and the case the later Iowa-circuit authorities (Stanley v. Finnegan, Webster, Mitchell) build on. Its omission leaves DEC-04, INP-12 and FAIL-02 resting entirely on decisions from 2005 forward with no account of where the circuit's standard originated.
